source.title: How does Disagreement Help Generalization against Label Corruption?
source.authors: Xingrui Yu; Bo Han; Jiangchao Yao; Gang Niu; I. Tsang; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on noisy labels that refine the broad memorization claim: its methods rely on fitting clean labels before overfitting noisy labels, but it also reports that disagreement-only training cannot handle noisy labels effectively. It does not directly test the six claim versions as phrased.
record.gate_note: The paper's direct results concern test accuracy and divergence under label-corruption interventions, not zero training error on random labels, convergence time, unstructured inputs, perfectly fitting every noise fraction, regularization ablations, or a direct comparison of learning real versus random labels. Reported Standard test-accuracy trends and the divergence comparison bear on the claim's subject but do not measure the named version outcomes. The many benchmark accuracy comparisons test robustness methods, not the original claim's outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own epoch-wise Standard test-accuracy trajectories on four datasets and explicitly interprets their early rise and later decline as learning clean labels before overfitting noisy labels. These results bear indirectly on V6 in new settings. They do not establish perfect training fit, fully random-label memorization, or the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Co-teaching+ improves noisy-label robustness by combining small-loss selection, cross-updating, and maintained network disagreement. They also interpret Standard's early test-accuracy peak and later decline as clean-label learning followed by noisy-label overfitting.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses symmetric or pairwise label flips on benchmark datasets and compares methods for noisy-label robustness; it does not reproduce random-label memorization experiments or measure training error on random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and corruption pattern/rate vary; the divergence and test-accuracy results differ across methods and benchmark settings. CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and T-ImageNet use Co-teaching warm-up periods; Open-sets use parallel warm-up.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard T-ImageNet test accuracy is 35.56% at symmetric 20% corruption and 19.58% at symmetric 50% corruption; pairwise 45% corruption gives 26.14%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this training setup, increasing symmetric label corruption from 20% to 50% lowers final test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Disagreement training maintains output divergence between networks, whereas Co-teaching gradually produces consensus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Updating on prediction-disagreement examples can maintain divergence between two MNIST classifiers.

record.problems: The primary epoch-wise accuracy outcomes are presented in plots without numerical values in the supplied text; Table 4 reports selected aggregate test accuracies. Several Standard results in Table 5 are borrowed from Wang et al. (2018). The paper does not report training errors for its noisy-label experiments.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded the three Open-set Standard values from Table 5 because the text explicitly says they are borrowed from Wang et al. (2018), rather than results generated by this study. No other separately reported own results bearing on the catalog claim were omitted.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios and convergence speed as label corruption increases.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across noise fractions and a steady test-error trajectory from clean labels to fully random labels.
Regularization ablations testing random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Separate clean-example and corrupted-example training losses or accuracies over time; direct measurement of noise memorization; training on completely random labels.

record.verdict_notes: The primary contribution uses memorization effects for mitigation, but the study also reports untreated Standard trajectories bearing on V6. Those trajectories support the authors' temporal interpretation without directly establishing when corrupted training labels are fitted. Mitigation performance and inter-network divergence do not themselves test the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment assigns completely random labels and reports training error or chance-level test error.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed across label-corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
Experiments report test accuracy at selected corruption settings; they do not report perfect training fit across a sweep from clean to fully random labels.
No weight-decay, dropout, or augmentation ablation on random labels or true-label generalization.
The paper describes memorization effects and plots test accuracy over epochs under label noise, but does not directly measure whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: 3-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared total variation of Softmax outputs between two networks trained under the Disagreement strategy for 10 trials.
rows.measure: Total Variation of Softmax outputs between networks
rows.value: Figure 1 reports a divergence curve; exact values are figure-only. Text says networks trained by the Disagreement strategy often keep diverged.
rows.note: This measures divergence, not any outcome in V1–V6; comparison with Co-teaching is in the same figure and described textually.
rows.check: Output divergence between networks is observed, but it cannot determine any V1–V6 effect.

relationships.condition: Standard training on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and NEWS with symmetric 20%/50% or pairwise 45% corruption
relationships.reason: R1–R12 show early high test accuracy followed by decline, explicitly interpreted by the authors as clean-label learning before noisy-label overfitting; support is indirect because separate clean/noisy training fits are not measured.
relationships.display_finding: Early high test accuracy was followed by decline, which the authors interpreted as clean-label learning before noisy-label overfitting.
